title: Functions and script arguments
goal: Write reusable functions that return data the right way, and scripts that accept options, check input and print a clear usage message.
setup: # P5: files of known size, one name with a space

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Print the size in KB of each file given as an argument, then the total.' 'total=0' 'to_kb() {' '  size=$(stat -c %s "$1")' '  return $(( size / 1024 ))' '}' 'for f in $*; do' '  to_kb "$f"' '  kb=$?' '  echo "$f: $kb KB"' '  total=$((total + kb))' 'done' 'echo "total: $total KB"' > sizes.sh

printf '%s\n' '# helpers.sh - shared functions. Load with: source helpers.sh' 'log()  { echo "[$(date +%H:%M:%S)] INFO  $*"; }' 'warn() { echo "[$(date +%H:%M:%S)] WARN  $*" >&2; }' 'die()  { echo "[$(date +%H:%M:%S)] ERROR $*" >&2; exit 1; }' > helpers.sh

warmup.q: Why does `cat file | while read x; do n=$((n+1)); done; echo $n` print an empty or 0 value?
warmup.a: The pipe runs the loop in a subshell. Use `while ...; done < file` instead.

warmup.q: How do you get the number of items in the array `IMAGES`?

warmup.a: Use the first argument, or `0` if it is empty or missing.

warmup.q: Single or double quotes for `echo "Hello $USER"`, and why?
warmup.a: Double quotes, so `$USER` is replaced. Single quotes would print `$USER` literally.

problems.title: return vs echo: get a value out of a function
problems.situation: A teammate wrote `get_port() { return 8080; }` and the script tries to connect to port 144. Interviewers love this one: in bash, `return` gives only an exit code (0-255). Real data must be printed with `echo` and caught with `$( )`.
task: Define `get_port() { return 8080; }`. Call it, then print `$?`. What number do you get?
Define `get_port() { echo 8080; }`. Save the result with `PORT=$(get_port)` and print it.
Write `is_port_open()` that uses `return 0` or `return 1`, and use it in an `if`.
Explain in one sentence when to use `return` and when to use `echo`.
hints: Exit codes are 8 bits: 8080 is taken modulo 256.
Data = `echo` + `$(func)`. Success or failure = `return 0` / `return 1` + `if func`.
solution: get_port() { return 8080; }          # WRONG: return is only an exit code
get_port() { echo 8080; }            # RIGHT: print the data
if is_port_open "$PORT"; then echo "port $PORT is open"; fi

explanation.meaning: Ends the function with exit code N (0-255). Read it with `$?` or use the function in `if`.
8080 modulo 256 = 144. The value is silently wrong.
The function prints the data; `$( )` catches the output into a variable.
`if` looks at the exit code: 0 = true.
A variable only for this function. Inside a function, `$1` is the function's first argument.

problems.expected_output:
return gave: 144
echo gave: 8080
port 8080 is open
port 22 is closed
mistakes: Printing debug messages with `echo` inside a function that returns data with `echo`: the debug text ends up in the variable. Send debug text to stderr: `echo "debug" >&2`.
problems.interview_say: In bash, `return` only sets the exit code from 0 to 255, so I use it for success or failure. To return data, the function prints it with `echo` and the caller captures it with `$(func)`.
problems.try_yourself: Run `f() { echo data; echo debug >&2; }; X=$(f); echo "X=[$X]"`. Where does `debug` go?

problems.title: Predict: local vs global variables
problems.situation: A deploy script loops over servers with `i`, and calls a helper that also uses `i`. After the helper runs, the main loop is broken. Bash variables are global by default, even inside functions.
task: Read the code in the solution box only after you predict: `count_to_2() { for i in 1 2; do :; done; }`.
Predict, then run: `i=10; count_to_2; echo "i=$i"`.
Predict, then run the same with `local i` inside the function.
Predict, then run: a function that sets `RESULT=done` (no local). Is `RESULT` visible after the call?
hints: Without `local`, the function changes the global `i`.
`local i` makes a new `i` that exists only while the function runs.
A global set inside a function stays after the call.
solution: count_to_2() { for i in 1 2; do :; done; }
count_to_2() { local i; for i in 1 2; do :; done; }

explanation.meaning: The function uses the same global `i`. After the loop, `i` is 2.
A separate `i` for the function only. The global `i` keeps 10.
Global again: visible after the call. Sometimes useful, often a surprise.
A command that does nothing. Here it is the empty loop body.

problems.expected_output:
without local: i=2
with local:    i=10
RESULT=done
mistakes: Using `local` outside a function: `bash: local: can only be used in a function`.
`local x=$(cmd)` hides the exit code of `cmd` (`$?` is the exit code of `local`). Write `local x; x=$(cmd)` when the exit code matters.

checks.expect: local: can only be used in a function

problems.interview_say: Variables in bash are global by default, also inside functions. I declare every function variable with `local` so helpers do not break the caller's variables.
problems.try_yourself: Run `f() { local x; x=$(false); echo $?; }; f` and `g() { local x=$(false); echo $?; }; g`. Why are the numbers different?

problems.title: getopts: a deploy script with options
problems.situation: The team wants `deploy.sh -e staging -v 2.4.1 [-n]`: `-e` environment (required), `-v` version (default `latest`), `-n` dry run. Wrong input must show a usage message and exit 2. This is how real CLI tools behave.
task: Write a `usage()` function that prints the usage to stderr and exits 2.
Parse options with `while getopts "e:v:nh" opt; do case $opt in ... esac; done`.
Set defaults: `VERSION=latest`, `DRY_RUN=false`. Check that `-e` was given and is `dev`, `staging` or `prod`.
Print `deploy VERSION to ENV (dry run: yes/no)`.
Test: `-e staging -v 2.4.1`, `-n -e prod`, no options, `-e test`, and `-x`. Print the exit code each time.
hints: In `"e:v:nh"`, a colon after a letter means "this option needs a value". The value is in `$OPTARG`.
`\?)` handles unknown options (getopts prints its own error first).
After the loop, check: `[ -n "$ENV" ] || usage` and `case $ENV in dev|staging|prod) ;; *) usage ;; esac`.
solution: case $ENV in dev|staging|prod) ;; *) echo "error: unknown environment '$ENV'" >&2; usage ;; esac

explanation.meaning: Read one option per loop round into `opt`. `e:` and `v:` need a value; `n` and `h` do not.
The value of the current option, for example `staging`.
getopts sets `opt` to `?` for an unknown option or a missing value.
One place for the help text. Exit 2 = wrong usage.
Options only overwrite them when given.
Required options and allowed values are checked once, at the end.

problems.expected_output:
deploy 2.4.1 to staging (dry run: false)
exit: 0
deploy latest to prod (dry run: true)
exit: 0
usage: deploy.sh -e <dev|staging|prod> [-v version] [-n]
exit: 2
error: unknown environment 'test'
usage: deploy.sh -e <dev|staging|prod> [-v version] [-n]
exit: 2
deploy.sh: illegal option -- x
usage: deploy.sh -e <dev|staging|prod> [-v version] [-n]
exit: 2
mistakes: Forgetting the colon: `getopts "ev:n"` and `-e staging` sets nothing, and `staging` is left as a normal argument.
Using `$1`, `$2` by hand for options: it breaks when the user changes the order. getopts handles any order.
getopts only supports short options like `-e`. For `--env`, use a `while`/`case`/`shift` loop (see P4).
problems.interview_say: For script options I use `getopts`, set defaults first, validate required values after the loop, and call a `usage` function that prints to stderr and exits with code 2.
problems.try_yourself: Add `-r replicas` with a default of 2, and reject values that are not numbers using `[[ $REPLICAS =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]`.

problems.title: "$@" vs "$*", and shift
problems.situation: A wrapper script `kube.sh` passes all its arguments to another command. One argument contains a space (a label value). Only `"$@"` keeps every argument exactly. `shift` is used to take off the first word (a subcommand).
task: Write `show_args() { for a in "$@"; do echo "[$a]"; done; }`.
Call a function with `"$@"`, with `"$*"`, and with `$@` (no quotes), passing: `get pods "app=todo api"`.
Use `shift` to read a subcommand: `cmd=$1; shift`, then print the subcommand and the rest.
Print `$#` before and after `shift`.
hints: `"$@"` = each argument as a separate word, exactly as given.
`"$*"` = all arguments joined into ONE word. `$@` without quotes splits at spaces again.
`shift` removes `$1`; then `$2` becomes `$1`, and `$#` is one smaller.
solution: show_args() { for a in "$@"; do echo "  [$a]"; done; }

explanation.meaning: Each argument separate and unchanged. Use this to pass arguments on.
All arguments as one string (joined with spaces). Good for messages only.
Split again at spaces: `app=todo api` becomes two words. A bug.
Drop the first argument. Common for `tool.sh <subcommand> <args...>`.

problems.expected_output:
with "$@":
  [get]
  [pods]
  [app=todo api]
with "$*":
  [get pods app=todo api]
with $@ (no quotes):
  [get]
  [pods]
  [app=todo]
  [api]
args: 3
subcommand: deploy, rest: 2
  [staging]
  [v2 final]
mistakes: Writing `exec kubectl $@` in a wrapper: arguments with spaces break. Always `"$@"`.
Calling `shift` when there are no arguments: nothing happens and the exit code is 1. Check `$#` first.
problems.interview_say: `"$@"` passes every argument exactly as given, so I use it in wrappers. `"$*"` joins them into one string. `shift` removes the first argument, which is handy for subcommands.
problems.try_yourself: Write a loop `while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do echo "arg: $1"; shift; done` inside a function and call it with 4 arguments.

problems.title: Find the bug: the file size helper
problems.situation: `sizes.sh` should print the size in KB of each file and the total. For `big.log` (300 KB) it says 44 KB, and `my notes.txt` gives an error. The function uses `return` for data.
task: Run `bash sizes.sh big.log small.log "my notes.txt"`. Compare with `ls -l`.
Find 3 bugs: data returned with `return`, `$*` in the loop, and a variable that should be `local`.
Fix them and run again.
hints: 300 % 256 = 44. That is the `return` problem from P1.
`for f in $*` splits `my notes.txt` into two words. Use `"$@"`.
Inside the function: `local size`. Print the result with `echo`, catch it with `kb=$(to_kb "$f")`.
solution: # Print the size in KB of each file given as an argument, then the total.

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: print the number. `return 300` became 44.
Catch the printed number. `|| { ...; continue; }` skips files that fail.
Bug 2: `$*` split `my notes.txt` into `my` and `notes.txt`.
Bug 3: `size` was global and could clash with the caller.

problems.expected_output:
big.log: 44 KB
small.log: 5 KB
stat: cannot statx 'my': No such file or directory
my: 0 KB
stat: cannot statx 'notes.txt': No such file or directory
notes.txt: 0 KB
total: 49 KB
--- fixed ---
big.log: 300 KB
small.log: 5 KB
my notes.txt: 2 KB
total: 307 KB
problems.output_note: On Ubuntu 22.04 the error says `cannot stat` instead of `cannot statx` (older coreutils). The rest is the same.
mistakes: Seeing `stat: cannot statx 'my': No such file or directory` and renaming the file. The script must handle spaces.
Keeping `return` and adding `* 256`. Exit codes are never for data.

checks.expect: stat: cannot statx 'my': No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: I return data with `echo` and capture it with `$( )`, loop over `"$@"` so file names with spaces work, and declare function variables `local`.
problems.try_yourself: Add a check at the top: if no files are given, print `usage: sizes.sh FILE...` to stderr and exit 2.

problems.title: Input validation: required, defaults, numbers
problems.situation: A scale script takes `scale.sh <service> [replicas]`. The service is required. Replicas default to 2, must be a whole number, and must be between 1 and 10, or the cluster could be overloaded.
task: Use `${1:?message}` to stop when the service is missing.
Use `${2:-2}` for the default number of replicas.
Reject non-numbers with `[[ $R =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]` and values outside 1-10.
Test with: no args, `todo-api`, `todo-api 5`, `todo-api five`, `todo-api 50`.
hints: `${1:?service name is required}` prints the message and exits the script (code 1) when `$1` is empty.
Use `(( R >= 1 && R <= 10 ))` for the range check.
Send errors to `>&2` and use `exit 2` for bad input.
solution: [[ $R =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "error: replicas must be a number, got '$R'" >&2; exit 2; }
(( R >= 1 && R <= 10 )) || { echo "error: replicas must be 1-10, got $R" >&2; exit 2; }

explanation.meaning: If `$1` is empty or missing: print `msg` to stderr and exit.
Default value 2 when the second argument is missing.
Only digits, at least one.
Range check with normal math operators.

problems.expected_output:
scale.sh: line 2: 1: service name is required
exit: 1
kubectl scale deployment/todo-api --replicas=2
exit: 0
kubectl scale deployment/todo-api --replicas=5
exit: 0
error: replicas must be a number, got 'five'
exit: 2
error: replicas must be 1-10, got 50
exit: 2
mistakes: Checking the range before the number check: `(( five >= 1 ))` treats `five` as an empty variable (0) and gives a confusing result.
Forgetting that `${1:?}` exits the whole script, not only the function.
problems.interview_say: I validate input at the top of the script: required arguments with `${1:?msg}`, defaults with `${2:-value}`, and numbers with a regex and a range check, so bad input never reaches kubectl.
problems.try_yourself: Change the default to come from an environment variable: `R=${2:-${DEFAULT_REPLICAS:-2}}`. Test with `DEFAULT_REPLICAS=3 bash scale.sh todo-api`.

problems.title: A shared function library with source
problems.situation: Every team script has the same `log`, `warn` and `die` functions copied in. A better way: keep them in one file `helpers.sh` and load it with `source`. Then all scripts print messages in the same format.
task: Read `helpers.sh`.
Write `job.sh` that does `source "$(dirname "$0")/helpers.sh"`, then calls `log`, `warn`, and `die` if a file is missing.
Run `bash job.sh` and print the exit code. Send stderr to `/dev/null` once to see the difference.
hints: `$(dirname "$0")` is the folder of the script, so `source` works from any folder.
`warn` and `die` print to stderr; `die` also exits with code 1.
`[ -f config.yml ] || die "config.yml not found"`.

explanation.meaning: Load the functions into the current script.
The script's own folder, so the path works from anywhere.
Print an error and stop. Very common helper.
In a message function, `$*` joins all words into one line.

problems.expected_output:
[15:59:16] INFO  backup job started
[15:59:16] WARN  disk is 85% full
[15:59:16] ERROR config.yml not found
exit: 1
--- stderr hidden ---
[15:59:16] INFO  backup job started
exit: 1
problems.output_note: The time in brackets is the current time, so it is different on every run.
mistakes: `source helpers.sh` with a relative path: it fails when the script is started from another folder (`helpers.sh: No such file or directory`).
Putting `exit` in a sourced library outside a function: it ends the script that sources it.

checks.run: mkdir -p other && cd other && printf 'source helpers.sh\n' > j.sh && bash j.sh
checks.expect: helpers.sh: No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: I keep shared functions like `log` and `die` in one file and load it with `source`. Errors go to stderr, so tools that read stdout get clean data.
problems.try_yourself: Add a `debug()` function that only prints when `DEBUG=1` is set. Test with `DEBUG=1 bash job.sh`.

interview.q: How do you return a string from a bash function?
interview.a: Print it with `echo` and capture it with `VAR=$(func)`. `return` only sets an exit code from 0 to 255.
It makes a variable that exists only inside the function, so it does not change a global variable with the same name.

interview.q: What is the difference between `"$@"` and `"$*"`?
interview.a: `"$@"` keeps each argument separate and unchanged. `"$*"` joins all arguments into one string.

interview.q: How do you parse options like `-e staging -v 2.4` in bash?
interview.a: With `while getopts "e:v:" opt; do case $opt in e) ENV=$OPTARG;; ... esac; done`. A colon means the option needs a value.

interview.q: What should a script do when it gets wrong input?
interview.a: Print a short usage message to stderr and exit with a non-zero code, usually 2.

recap.meaning: Get data from a function (it echoes)
Required argument, else exit with msg
